sheet-2.description: Sheet 2 shows the commercial centre of Newton at 50 feet to an inch, with the drawing turned so that north lies towards the upper left. It is bounded by Trinity Street along the top and Moran Street at the right, and its left edge runs past Water, High and Academy Streets. Spring Street crosses the upper half from the curved junction with Water and Mill Streets to Moran Street, lined on its north side by a solid row of brick and frame stores and hotels numbered from 1 to 115 Spring Street: the Antlers Hotel, Earl's Hotel, the Cochran House, the Merchants National Bank, bakeries, jewelers, hardware and dry goods stores. The County Court House (built 1847), the Jail (built 1892) and the County Clerk and Surrogate's Office stand beside the Public Square, a large rectangle crossed by diagonal paths with a monument. Park Place runs along its south side, where the Park Block, Park Theatre, the Newton Trust Company, the Smith Building and the First M. E. Church face the square. South of them lie the First Presbyterian Church, a chapel, Christ Church (Episcopal) with its parish house, and the lots of Church Street. Main Street runs down the right side and High Street curves down the left past the Park Hotel, liveries, hotel stables and dwellings. The Hotel Newton and its horse sheds and carriage house fill the block between Mill and Spring Streets at the left. A No. 2 Chemical Engine Company note describes the apparatus kept at 44 High Street. Water pipe sizes, hydrants and fire alarm boxes are drawn in the streets, and the margins carry notes about two roofs on Spring Street buildings. The lower left edge is marked No Exposure.
notes: Water Street has been realigned: today NJ 94 follows a diagonal line to the west of Spring Street and the Public Square, so the old Water Street, Spring Street and Mill Street junction at the upper left has no matching junction in OpenStreetMap and was not used.
Park Place is now part of the Newton Traffic Circle around the Public Square; the sheet draws the south side of the Public Square as Park Place.
Linwood Annex is Linwood Annex Avenue today; the High Street on the sheet is High Street (CR 519) in OpenStreetMap.
A margin note on the sheet explains that the buildings at 67-69 and 103 Spring Street have two roofs, a false roof built over the original tin roof.

Placed from five automatically detected junctions (Spring, Moran, Main, Church, High and Academy Streets); the Trinity Street junctions were not detected because that boundary street is cut at the sheet edge.
Town centre: Spring, Main, High, Park Place, Church. One part, 50 ft. Water Street junction unused (NJ 94 realigned); rotation about -43.

sheet-3.description: Sheet 3 covers the blocks south and east of Newton's Public Square at 50 feet to an inch, with north towards the upper left. Spring Street crosses the upper third from Moran Street at the left to the sheet edge beyond Jefferson Street at the right. North of it lie the south ends of the blocks fronting Spring Street, where the sheet shows rear lots with garages, auto sheds, J. English's Sons machine and blacksmith shop, English Place and private driveways. South of Spring Street the business blocks run from the Sussex National Bank and the stores of Main Street, including the Newton Opera House, Post Office and printing office of the New Jersey Herald, to the Waldmere Hotel, the Number 1 Hose Company and Kittatinny Hose Company building, a garage drawn from plans, a livery stable and a sash and door warehouse. East of Adams Street a block of dwellings and a tea company store lies between Spring and Washington Streets, and A. B. Brickner's beer bottling and soda water works stands on Washington Street near Jefferson Street. The lower two thirds of the sheet is mostly open: the walled Old Newton Cemetery, the Catholic Cemetery, a lumber store, and scattered dwellings along Main Street and Halsted Street. Water pipe sizes, hydrants and fire alarm boxes are shown in the streets. The sheet is bounded by Moran Street at the top left, Main Street on the left, Halsted Street at the bottom and Jefferson Street at the right, and the Division Street and Church Street ends are lettered at the left edge.
notes: Church Street and Division Street are lettered only where they meet Main Street at the left edge of the sheet.
Park Place is lettered at the left edge as Park Pl.; today it is part of the Newton Traffic Circle.

Placed from nine automatically detected junctions with an RMSE of 2.2 m; the two Halsted Street junctions carry residuals of 3 to 4 m and pull the fitted scale about 1 percent below the fit without them. Medium confidence.
The private ways lettered Driveway are not streets.
Main, Spring, Adams, Washington, Halsted; old cemetery block. One part, 50 ft. Two Halsted Street junctions at 3 to 4 m kept.

sheet-4.description: Sheet 4 covers a residential district east of the Newton town centre at 50 feet to an inch, drawn with north towards the upper left. It is bounded by Trinity Street along the top, Union Place and Hampton Street on the north and east, Halsted Street along the bottom and Jefferson Street on the west, whose far side belongs to sheet 3. Spring Street enters from the west, turns at Union Place and runs diagonally south-east across the sheet towards its junction with Cedar Street, Hampton Street and the head of Sparta Avenue at the lower right. Madison Street and Jefferson Street run north to south through the western half, crossed by Washington Street, and Cedar Street runs east from Madison Street towards Spring Street. Most lots hold frame dwellings of two to two and a half storeys with outbuildings, sheds and private garages. A row of small shops and flats lines the south side of the block between Trinity and Spring Streets, with a tailor and an optician near its west end. The large brick Public School, with its manual training building, laboratory and auditorium, fills much of the block between Cedar Street and Halsted Street, reached by an entrance to the school yard from Spring Street. The Hart and Iliff Company lumber yard with its sheds lies between Spring Street and Hampton Street, John Farrell and Son's machine shop stands on the east side of Madison Street, and a boarding house lettered "The Homeste" stands on Union Place. Water pipes and their diameters are drawn along most streets, with fire alarm boxes and hydrants. The north-east of the sheet is largely open ground.
notes: The boarding house on Union Place is lettered "The Homeste" (cut off); the index lists it as "Homeste, The".
Sparta Avenue is lettered only in part at the lower right edge.

Today Union Place, Madison Street and Spring Street meet at a single OpenStreetMap node, while the sheet draws Union Place meeting Spring Street about 60 ft east of Madison Street; that junction was left out of the fit.
Pilot. Trinity, Union Place, Spring, Madison, Jefferson, Washington, Cedar, Halsted, Hampton; public school. One part, 50 ft. Rotation about -42 deg.

sheet-5.description: Sheet 5 shows the eastern edge of Newton's built-up area at 50 feet to an inch, with north towards the upper left. Trinity Street crosses the top third, with Hampton Street running down the left side to the corner where it joins Spring Street, the Lackawanna Hotel and Garage and the Hart and Iliff Company's lumber, coal and building material yard at the lower left. The Hart and Iliff yard fills the block between Hampton Street and the railroad, with coal pockets under a car shed, a feed and grain warehouse, lumber sheds and a wood saw run by an electric motor. The Sussex branch of the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad, lettered S.R.R. of N.J., runs from top to bottom with a spur and sidings, and a short Railroad Avenue follows its west side. The Ideal Dairy Company, a milk bottling works formerly the Thorndale Farms Creamery, stands east of the tracks with an ice house and drives, and a Town Stone Crushing Plant, seldom used, stands near the top. Stuart Street curves down the right side from Trinity Street to its junction with Diller Avenue, and Palmer Street and Mt. View Avenue bound the open fields and scattered dwellings on the right. Dwellings with private garages and sheds line Hampton, Stuart and Diller Avenue, and a large factory building stands at the bottom edge near Diller Avenue. Water pipes and their sizes are drawn along the streets.
notes: Railroad Avenue does not exist today; the railroad is abandoned (the Sussex Branch Trail follows part of it).
The stretch lettered Diller Av. west of Stuart Street is part of Spring Street today; Mt. View Av. is Mount View Street today.

Placed from three detected junctions (Hampton and Trinity, Palmer and Stuart, Mount View and Palmer) and one hand-picked point at Stuart and Diller Avenue; the fit gives a scale about 3.5 percent above the atlas value. Low confidence.
The OpenStreetMap node for Hampton Street and Spring Street lies on the sheet edge and was not used.
Trinity, Hampton, Stuart, Mt. View Av, Palmer, Spring, Railroad Av, Diller; rail line. One part, 50 ft. 4 points (1 hand-picked Diller/Spring/Stuart); fitted scale 3.4 percent above the atlas.

sheet-6.description: Sheet 6 shows the north-western edge of Newton along Mill Street at 50 feet to an inch, with north towards the upper left. Mill Street crosses the sheet from the left edge to the right, where it meets Water Street, and the south side is built up with a row of narrow lots and frame dwellings numbered from 5 to 38 Mill Street. A larger group of buildings lies at the right edge: the Hotel Sussex, a hotel stable, A. B. Koyt's wagon works and garage, an auto repair and storage building and J. M. Kishpaugh's garage along Water Street. The Standard Towel Company mill stands on the north side of Mill Street at the left, with a weaving room, stock and folding room and a watchman's clock system, and an old ice house lies north of it. Long narrow lots run north from Mill Street to a brook that crosses the upper part of the sheet. Harrison Street runs south from Mill Street between a block bounded by Cherry Street and the lots of the Mill Street frontage, and Center Street runs across the lower part of the sheet. A block of dwellings enclosed by Cherry Street, Harrison Street and Center Street is lettered 30. The lower right of the sheet has a lettered Not Named street, open ground, and a few large frame buildings, and the margins at the lower left are marked No Exposure. Pipe sizes and hydrants are drawn along the streets.
notes: A street lettered Not Named runs south from Mill Street near the lower centre of the sheet; it has no name on the map and was not used.
The modern Mill Street line lies about 4 m south of the drawn street where it meets Harrison Street (residual 3.8 m); the other junction residuals are 0.8 to 4.8 m.
Placed from four junctions on Harrison, Cherry, Center and Mill Streets, all in the left half of the sheet and with a fitted rotation of about -55 degrees; low confidence.
The brook crossing the upper part of the sheet is lettered Brook.
Mill, Center, Cherry, Harrison, High; brook. One part, 50 ft. 4 points, all in the left half; rotation about -55. Water Street at the right edge realigned, not used.

sheet-7.description: Sheet 7 shows the eastern edge of the Newton town centre at 50 feet to an inch, drawn with north towards the upper left. The main area is the lower and right part of the page. Clinton Street runs across the lower left from the left edge towards the junction at the right, where it meets Water Street and East Clinton Street at a fire alarm box. Water Street runs the full height of the right side with scattered frame dwellings on the lots to its east, a shed, and a barn at the upper right. Emmans Avenue runs from the heavy-lined edge of the sheet down to Clinton Street, with a row of dwellings on its west side. The largest feature is the commercial greenhouse range of Geo. M. Emmans, a group of long glass houses and a hot bed set in a fan beside Emmans Avenue, heated by steam, lit by lanterns and one acetylene lamp, with a boiler and coal house, pot storage and an office. At the lower right, near the junction, stand the Sussex Steam Laundry and the Broda-Newton garage in a brick building coloured as fire-resistive, with auto storage buildings beside it and a note about a building to be moved to the location shown. A brook crosses the lower centre and another runs in from the right edge beside East Clinton Street. A short stretch of Hamilton Street is lettered at the bottom edge. The upper left corner of the page, cut off by a heavy line and marked No Exposure, shows a separate piece of Clinton Street drawn at a different angle with its own compass and is not part of this mask.
notes: Emmans Avenue is Emmons Avenue today.
The heavy-lined area at upper left, with its own Clinton Street and north arrow, is a separate piece that has no street junction and was not georeferenced.
The part is placed by two detected junctions and one hand-picked junction (Hamilton Street and Water Street); treat the fit as low confidence.

Clinton, E. Clinton, Water, Emmans Av (Emmons Avenue today); brook, commercial greenhouses. Heavy line at upper left marks the drawn edge. 50 ft. One placed part (3 points, 1 hand-picked at Hamilton / Water). Part 2: upper-left patch behind the heavy line, another stretch of Clinton Street, unplaced.

Not georeferenced on this sheet: upper-left patch behind the heavy line: another stretch of Clinton Street, with its own compass (no street junction; needs step 6b: carried points from sheet 6 or parcel block corners).

sheet-8.description: Sheet 8 covers the blocks between Water Street at the top and Townsend Street at the bottom, at 50 feet to an inch, drawn with north towards the upper right. Trinity Street runs down the left side, Hamilton Street divides the upper block from top to Moran Street, and East Clinton Street bounds the area on the right. Moran Street crosses the lower middle. The upper blocks are closely built with frame dwellings, mostly two and a half storeys, on narrow lots numbered along Trinity and Hamilton Streets. At the upper left corner, on Water Street, stands the Wm. H. Earl beer bottling and soda water works, with storage, heated by steam and lit by electric and gas lights, and a blacksmith and wheelwright and printing premises beside it. A roller skating rink, noted as seldom used, stands at the top near Water Street beside a brook. Further down on East Clinton Street the buildings of the former gas works are drawn in pink and labelled vacant, with a storage building for farm implements beside them. Below Moran Street the blocks are mostly open ground with a few dwellings, a long shed, and, at the lower right, the Newton Embroidery Works, a brick factory with a boiler plant and gasoline engine, steam heat and electric light. Lots and dwellings line the north side of Townsend Street at the bottom edge. A compass in the upper right shows north to the upper right. A brook crosses the upper right corner.
notes: The sheet is drawn with Water Street along the top, turned about 47 degrees from north.
Several of the junctions are placed from a single drawn edge (Water Street and Townsend Street are cut by the sheet edges).
Townsend, Moran, Hamilton, Water, E. Clinton, Trinity. One part, 50 ft. Turned about +47 deg.

sheet-9-1.description: The main part of sheet 9 covers the thinly built district north-east of Trinity Street, drawn at 50 feet to an inch and turned on the page so that Trinity Street runs down the left edge and north points to the upper right. Townsend Street runs along the top of the sheet and Union Place crosses it from Trinity Street towards the east, parallel to Townsend Street. Hampton Street meets Trinity Street at the lower left, lettered just inside the edge. Frame dwellings of two to two and a half storeys, with small stables, sheds and private garages, line Townsend Street, both sides of Union Place and the east side of Trinity Street; a greenhouse stands behind the houses of Union Place. The interior of the large block between Union Place and the lower edge is almost entirely open ground, with only a few scattered outbuildings and a wagon house. Water pipes with their diameters run along Townsend Street, Union Place and Trinity Street, and street widths of 40 and 60 feet are noted. A heavy line divides the lower right of the sheet from two separately drawn insets, one of the Newton Gas and Electric Company works beside the railroad and one of the Sussex Photo Supply Company on Lafayette Road; those insets are not part of this area. The lower part of the area, towards the heavy dividing line, is left blank.
notes: Placed from three junctions along Trinity Street only (a helmert fit); position across Trinity Street is well fixed, rotation rests on points along one line.

Three parts. Part 1 main: Trinity (down the left edge), Townsend, Union Place; turned about 90 deg against sheet 4. Part 2 inset: Newton Gas & Electric Co. works beside the railroad (no street). Part 3 inset: Sussex Photo Supply Co. on Lafayette Road (Germany Flats Road) at Sparta Av.

Not georeferenced on this sheet: inset: Newton Gas & Electric Co. works beside the Sussex Railroad (no street junction; only abandoned rail lines; needs parcel corners or carried points from sheet 11 or 14).

Not georeferenced on this sheet: inset: Sussex Photo Supply Co. on Lafayette Road (Germany Flats Road) at Sparta Avenue (one junction whose modern identity is uncertain (road since realigned along the old rail bed, Hicks Avenue / Warbasse Junction Road); needs identification of Lafayette Road today, then an anchored part).

sheet-10.description: Sheet 10 is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north towards the upper left and covers the railroad yard and depot district south-east of the Newton town centre. Sparta Avenue runs diagonally down the left side and Spring Street crosses the upper left corner; Diller Avenue runs from the top, where Stuart Street leaves it, down to the lower right, and New Hampshire Avenue branches from it towards the upper right. Railroad Avenue runs diagonally through the middle of the sheet beside the tracks, and Woodside Avenue meets Sparta Avenue at the bottom. The centre is taken up by the yard of the Sussex Railroad, a branch of the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad, with many parallel tracks, the freight house and passenger station near the top, and a round house with a turntable at the left. Between the tracks and Diller Avenue stand the lumber, coal, feed and building materials yard of the L. S. Iliff Company, with its sheds and warehouses, and the mill of the Milliken-Kellam Company, makers of fly screens and general millwork. Frame dwellings of two to two and a half storeys, with stables and garages, line Sparta Avenue, Railroad Avenue, Diller Avenue and New Hampshire Avenue, and the upper right of the sheet is a loosely built residential area with driveways reaching into the blocks. Water pipes, hydrants and fire alarm boxes are shown.
notes: Railroad Avenue has no counterpart in today's street network; the railroad through the yard is abandoned (the Sussex Branch Trail follows part of it).
The stretch lettered Diller Avenue at the top of the sheet, west of Stuart Street, is part of Spring Street today.
Placed from three points, two of them hand-picked (Sparta Avenue / Woodside Avenue and the Spring Street, Diller Avenue and Stuart Street junction); low confidence.
Railroad yard: Sparta Av, Spring, Diller Av, Stuart St, New Hampshire Av, Railroad Av, Woodside Av; round house, depots, L. S. Iliff Co., Milliken-Kellam Co. One part, 50 ft; few junctions.

sheet-11.description: Sheet 11 shows the Sussex Print Works and Valentine and Bentley silk mill district on the south-eastern side of Newton, at 50 feet to an inch, drawn with north towards the upper right. Woodside Avenue runs along the top, Pine Street down the left edge and Sparta Avenue down the right side of the main block, while Merriam Avenue crosses diagonally below the mill and Sussex Street runs diagonally along the bottom. The middle of the sheet is filled by the large brick works of the Sussex Print Works and Valentine and Bentley Silk Company, with weaving and quilling, carpet cleaning and repair shops, card perforating, stock room, dye house, steaming room, silk cloth printing and boiler and engine rooms, protected by private hydrants, hose, automatic sprinklers and fire pails, and noted as mutual risk with admission refused and plans copied from a former survey. Frame dwellings stand along Pine and Woodside, in the upper left, and in a row along Sussex Street, with wood sheds and chicken houses along the rear lot line. At the right, across Sparta Avenue, are the buildings of the H. W. Merriam Shoe Company, also mutual risk, with a storage building and oil house, bounded on the east by Diller Avenue and the railroad of the Delaware Lackawanna and Western branch (lettered S. R. R. of N. J.). Water pipes are drawn along the streets. A compass at upper right shows north to the upper right.
notes: The railroad at the right edge is lettered S. R. R. of N. J. (Branch of D. L. and W. R. R.).
Railroad Avenue, lettered at the upper right, does not exist today.
Diller, Sparta, Merriam, Sussex, Pine; Merriam shoe factory, Valentine & Bentley silk. One part, 50 ft.

sheet-12-1.description: Sheet 12 shows the west side of Newton at 100 feet to an inch, drawn with north towards the upper left. This part covers most of the page. Main Street runs down the right side and High Street crosses the upper left, running diagonally from Church Street at the top to West End Avenue and beyond to the lower left edge. Between them Church, Division, Liberty, Thompson, Clarkson and Foster Streets cross Linwood Avenue and its upper extension, Annex, with Franklin Street, Dunn Place, South Avenue and West End Avenue (also lettered Love Lane) to the west and Ryerson Avenue and Ashford Street at the lower right. The upper blocks near Church, Division and Liberty Streets are the most closely built, with frame dwellings and a row of shops at the north end, a historical society building and the First Baptist Church at Main Street. Newton Military Academy, a boarding school for boys heated by steam and lit by electricity, with a dormitory, class rooms, drill room and bowling alley, stands at the upper left beside Academy Street. The southern blocks, numbered 107 to 109, are largely open ground with scattered dwellings, Ward's greenhouses near Ashford Street, and houses along Foster Street. Water pipes and fire alarm boxes are drawn on most streets. The compass at the upper right shows north to the upper left. The lower left corner of the page, behind a heavy line, is a separate part.
notes: High Street is High Street (CR 519) and High Street in OpenStreetMap, with Academy Street meeting it twice.
Annex is the upper part of Linwood Annex Avenue today.
South Avenue is not in the OpenStreetMap extract and was left out of the fit.
Foster Street junctions carry residuals of 3 to 6 m, so the southern part of the sheet may be drawn slightly out of scale.

West side at 100 ft: Main, High, Academy, Liberty, Division, Linwood, Thompson, Franklin, Clarkson, Foster, Ashford, West End Av, South Av, Shady Lane. Heavy line lower left. Part 1 main; part 2 lower-left patch behind the heavy line (High Street / Shady Lane), anchored on one hand-picked point.

sheet-12-2.description: Part 2 of sheet 12 is the area at the lower left of the page, cut off from the main map by a heavy line and the words No Exposure along it, and drawn at its own angle with its own north arrow pointing to the upper left. It shows High Street running diagonally from the lower left to the heavy line at the right, with Shady Lane curving in from the upper left to meet it at the right edge of the part. The scale is 100 feet to an inch, like the rest of the sheet. High Street carries a 10 inch water pipe and is lettered 40 and 50 feet wide at different places; its house numbers run from 125 to 133 on this part. A handful of frame dwellings stand along Shady Lane and High Street, with outbuildings, and a single building coloured blue is drawn in the open ground between them. The block numbers 37A, 129 and 130 are lettered in the open ground, and the sheet number 12 is printed at the right edge. Most of the part is blank, outlined only by the lot lines, as a margin of the drawing. The corner of the main map beyond the heavy line repeats the same junction of High Street and Shady Lane at a different angle.
notes: This part repeats the High Street and Shady Lane junction that is also drawn on part 1 at a different angle; it is placed by that one hand-picked junction with the scale taken from part 1 and rotation from High Street, so it is low confidence.
Its own north arrow points about 36 degrees to the upper left; High Street gives about 27 degrees.

West side at 100 ft: Main, High, Academy, Liberty, Division, Linwood, Thompson, Franklin, Clarkson, Foster, Ashford, West End Av, South Av, Shady Lane. Heavy line lower left. Part 1 main; part 2 lower-left patch behind the heavy line (High Street / Shady Lane), anchored on one hand-picked point.

sheet-13-1.description: The main part of sheet 13 is drawn at 100 feet to an inch, with north towards the upper left, and covers the south-central part of Newton between Halsted Street at the top and Lawnwood Avenue at the bottom. Main Street runs down the left side, turning south-east at its junction with Maple Avenue and Ryerson Avenue; Clarkson Street, Dunn Place, Foster Street, Ryerson Avenue and Barrett Avenue meet it from the west. Elm Street and Walker Street cross the upper part, and Maple Avenue and Madison Street run diagonally from Elm Street down to Main Street. The blocks along Halsted, Elm, Maple and Madison Streets are closely built with frame dwellings of two to two and a half storeys, sheds and private garages; St. Joseph's Roman Catholic Church stands on the south side of Halsted Street, and the Merriam Home for Retired Ministers, with its kitchen wing and conservatory, occupies a large lot between Main Street and Maple Avenue. Much of the centre and east of the sheet is a large open area lettered Cemetery, bounded on the east by Sparta Avenue, which runs from its junction with Halsted Street at the top towards Woodside Avenue. Woodside Avenue runs diagonally up the right side, with a row of dwellings between it and Pine Street, and Lawnwood Avenue curves along the bottom to Main Street. Water pipes, hydrants and street widths are noted throughout. A heavy line cuts off the lower right corner, which holds a separately drawn inset of the New Jersey Slate Company works on West End Avenue; that inset is not part of this area.
notes: Drawn at 100 ft to an inch, unlike sheets 2 to 11 at 50 ft.
Pine Street / Woodside Avenue is a hand-picked point.

sheet-14-1.description: The main part of sheet 14 is drawn at 100 feet to an inch with north straight up, and covers the southern edge of Newton between Main Street on the left and Pine Street on the right. Main Street runs down the left side and ends at Woodside Avenue, which runs diagonally from the lower left, where it continues as a road out of town, up to Pine Street at the upper right. Lawnwood Avenue leaves Main Street near the top and runs south-east to meet Woodside Avenue, and Nelson Street runs from Main Street down to Woodside Avenue. Frame dwellings of one and a half to two and a half storeys, with chicken houses, sheds and a few private garages, line Main Street, Nelson Street, Lawnwood Avenue and both sides of Woodside Avenue; a motorcycle shop and a motorcycle repair shop stand on Woodside Avenue near Nelson Street. Much of the interior of the large blocks is open ground, and the upper part, north of Lawnwood Avenue, is the southern end of the cemetery. Water pipes, hydrants, fire alarm boxes and street widths of 35 to 50 feet are noted. Heavy lines separate this part from a separately drawn area along the top and right edges (Sussex Street, Orchard Street and Sparta Avenue) and from the inset of Morningside Park at the lower right; the margins along those lines are marked no exposure.
notes: Woodside Avenue continues south-west beyond Main Street as a road lettered only "Road" at the sheet edge.

sheet-14-2.description: The second part of sheet 14 is a separately drawn area along the top and right edges of the sheet, cut off from the main map by a heavy line, at 100 feet to an inch with its own north arrow pointing straight up. It covers the district east of the town centre between Pine Street and Sparta Avenue. Merriam Avenue crosses the upper left corner to meet Pine Street, which runs south-east past Sussex Street and Orchard Street; Sussex Street and Orchard Street run parallel to each other north-east to Sparta Avenue, which crosses the upper right of the part. The blocks between Pine Street, Sussex Street and Orchard Street are lined with frame dwellings of two to two and a half storeys, with chicken houses and private garages. Beyond Sparta Avenue the tracks of the Sussex Railroad of New Jersey and an oil car track run down the right side of the sheet; beside them stands the Standard Oil Company's depot, with tanks, a wagon house and an oil house of fireproof construction. Below the line of Sparta Avenue a narrow strip down the right edge shows scattered dwellings and stables reaching to Merriam Avenue at the bottom right. Water pipes, hydrants and street widths are noted.
notes: The railroad is lettered "S. R. R. of N. J." (Sussex Railroad of New Jersey); it is abandoned today.
The strip down the right edge, below Sparta Avenue, is included in this part because Sparta Avenue and the railroad continue into it without a break; it holds no junction of its own.

sheet-14-3.description: The third part of sheet 14 is an inset at the lower right of the sheet showing the Morningside Park development on the south-western edge of Newton, drawn at 100 feet to an inch with its own north arrow pointing to the upper left. It is bounded by a heavy line on the top and left, with its other margins marked no exposure. Condit Street and Fairview Avenue run across the inset, crossed by Ryerson Avenue and Plainfield Avenue, laying out a small grid of rectangular blocks with the name Morningside Park lettered across them. The blocks are only partly built up: scattered frame dwellings, one of brick stuccoed on hollow concrete block, an unfinished dwelling, and many chicken houses, sheds and private garages, including a cigar manufactory in a small building at the top left. Water pipes of four inches run along Condit Street, Ryerson Avenue, Fairview Avenue and Plainfield Avenue, and street widths of 50 feet are noted.
notes: The fitted scale of this inset is about 4 percent smaller than the main part of the sheet.
